newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa seeks early resumption of EU trade talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa seeks early resumption of EU trade talks.

text.p: South Africa wants a speedy resumption of stalled trade talks with the European Union after it broke an impasse last month by outlining its negotiating mandate to the EU, a government official said on Wednesday.
Department of Trade and Industry director of trade relations Bahle Sibisi said Pretoria was waiting for confirmation of dates from Brussels.
"We are waiting for the last, final word from Brussels, for the dates. There were tentative dates but they had a bit of a problem," Sibisi said by telephone from Pretoria.
He said the dates for the resumption of trade talks should be know later this week.
"We would rather have it sooner than later," he added.
The EU, which absorbs some 40 percent of South African imports and accounts for more than a third of South African imports, set out its negotiating mandate in March last year.
But Brussels' position was criticised by several influential parties in South Africa as being too harsh on the country and its southern African neighbours.
The EU has refused post-apartheid South Africa full accession to the Lome Convention which grants favourable access to its markets to developing countries in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

The EU produced a mandate which would exclude nearly 40 percent of South Africa's agricultural products from a future free trade deal, while calling on it to reduce tariffs to ensure easier access to its markets for European producers.

South African parliamentarians criticised this fiercely, claiming that the EU had failed to take into account the very different sizes and levels of development of the economies of the negotiating partners.
In turn, the EU criticised South Africa for dragging its heels in presenting its own position.

There have also been growing concerns within the southern Africa region about the impact of a free trade deal between Pretoria and Brussels on the economies of some of South Africa's smaller neighbours.
Other members of the five-nation South Africa Customs Union (SACU) -- Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Swaziland -- fear they will lose millions in income from the joint customs revenue pool.
